20517:
After Adam's suggestion yesterday, I figured I'd create an introduction post here.

My name is Evan Welty and I am a video game collector [shocking I know ;) ]. I have been collecting games since roughly 2011 when I was 11, and have always found the more obscure and older consoles more interesting.

I began researching the Bally Astrocade and its items in roughly 2018 and have been picking up pieces here and there when I can. I have a relatively large collection of very random and rare pieces for everything between Pong to PS5.

Personally, I love the idea of archiving the non-game items, such as papers, advertising, merchandise, and etc as it tends to get left behind. My personal collection focus currently is 70s-early 90s video game clothing (mainly atari), Atari 5200, and obscure and rare items from these consoles from the 70s and 80s. I hope to eventually create a book surrounding the merchandise from this era, along with their origins such as magazines and giveaways. I also am hoping to create some products for repair, such as a recreation of the BallyCheck that I personally own (Nitron).

If you happen to be around the Carolinas, you will likely see me often at Raleigh Retro Gamers events as I founded that Facebook group in 2018. I love sharing Bally stuff in the group when possible as many have never even heard of the console.

Thank you all for the efforts you have put into preserving this console as it is such a cool and interesting piece of history.

-Evan

I added instructions for 1982's "Omega Valley" by The Tiny Arcade. This AstroBASIC game was on Tape 101 with "Astro Terror."

https://ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/tiny_arcade/tiny_arcade.html#OmegaValleyInstructions

This game was archived by Paul Thacker on July 25, 2023, but I haven't yet added it to the Bally Alley website.  I hope to add it soon.  In the meantime, you can download it here:

https://groups.io/g/ballyalley/topic/100359584#20426

This is an unusual game, as it doesn't use the hand controllers at all.  Instead, you use the keypad to fire at the baddies.  Paul likes this game.  What do you think of it?

Here are the complete instructions for the game:

--------------------

OMEGA VALLEY
(One player)

Seated at the console of Omega Hydra 9's defense command center, you are alerted to a massive invasion of the three inhabited valleys of your planet. Your mission is to prevent the descending invaders from landing on the floors of the valleys by zapping them from the laser cannon emplacements in the walls. If three invaders land, they proclaim victory and the game is over.

Six aliens (from an invading force of eighteen) will descend upon each valley. Each group of six will present themselves in a different formation. When a creature comes within range of one of the four laser cannons, press the key on the keypad (from 1 to 4) with the same number of the cannon you wish to fire. The cannons are numbered near the side edges of the TV screen. (Note that they are placed in staggered or alternating fashion)

An invader can be eliminated by making a direct hit or by "grazing" the top or bottom of it. The creatures will always be eliminated from left to right- if two fall into your line of fire, the one furthest to the left will be zapped.

To assess the progress of each group of six attackers, you will have to switch views among the three valleys of Omega on your TV screen. To select the view you desire, use the three color-dot shift keys on the bottom row of the keypad. These keys are used as follows:

Press:              View:

Green Shift Key     Alpha Valley (Green Scenery)

Red Shift Key       Delta Valley (Red Scenery)

Blue Shift key      Omega Valley (Blue Scenery)

A marker box will appear over the name of the valley to give a further indication which one is being monitored.

If you survive the first wave of intruders (you guessed it!) eighteen more of their pals will show up, this time scattering their forces over a greater altitude range and descending at a faster rate. Each subsequent wave will increase their altitude range and, more gradually, their rate of descent.

SCORING

Each creature zapped is worth 10 points multiplied times the number of the wave which is descending. For example, at the start of each game an invader is worth 10 points. The next group is worth 10x2 or 20 points apiece, the next 30 points and so on.

BONUS SCORING

The days on Omega are shorter than the nights. If you hit six aliens during the daylight hours (when the sky is yellow) you receive 200 points times the wave score multiplier. (1st wave 200x1=200 points, 2nd wave 200x2=400 points, etc.) Once darkness falls again, the opportunity for bonus scoring is over until the next daylight period. (Be careful you don't get too carried away trying to garner bonus points and permit invaders to land.)

KEYPAD GAME
CONTROL SUMMARY

Keys 1 to 4          Fire laser cannons

Color shift keys     Green, Red & Blue keys select Alpha, Delta
                     and Omega valleys, respectively.

Your current score is shown in the upper right hand part of the screen, while the number of landings remaining is displayed in the upper left hand corner.

To start a new game, press any key on the keypad (except "H")

--------------------

Thanks to Evan for scanning this hard-to-find documentation.  Paul has these instructions too.  When he archives them, then I'll add them to this area of the Tiny Arcade instructions area of the website too.

I added alternate versions of the AstroBASIC program "3D Graphic Demo/Bit-Mapping Demo," a simple drawing program, by L&M Software released in 1982 that were archived from Nate Reeder's Astrocade collection in 2021 by Paul Thacker. The program's archive now also contains the AstroBASIC program listing and screenshots (which are attached to this post).

You can download the program's archive here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/l&m_software/l&m_software.html#3DGraphicsDemoBitMappingDemo

Here is the complete, yet very short, AstroBASIC program listing:

--------------------

001 print "                         "
002 SM=1;print "    PULL TAPE JACK CORD  ";for A=0to 2000;next A
004 print "   USE JOY STK #1 & TRIG.";for Z=0to 2000;next Z
006 print "BIT MAPPING UTILITY BY L&M";for B=0to 1000;next B
008 print "             ERASE CLEARS
010 SM=1;CY=-40
020 X=-80;Y=-17
030 NT=0;X=X+JX(1);Y=Y+JY(1);print "X",#2,X,;print "  Y",#2,Y
035 if &(21)=16goto 60
040 if TR(1)box X,Y,1,1,3;NT=3;MU=1;goto 30
050 box X,Y,1,1,3;box X,Y,1,1,3;goto 30
060 clear ;goto 10

--------------------

I don't believe that a useful BASIC program gets much shorter or simpler than this one.

A side effect of the way AstroBASIC does a memory dump is that you tend to get situations where multiple copies of a program have different binary data despite having no meaningful differences. A lot of programs archived long ago were copied by Mike White.

20531:
On August 6, 2023, Paul Thacker wrote, "A side effect of the way AstroBASIC does a memory dump is that you tend to get situations where multiple copies of a program have different binary data despite having no meaningful differences."

Yeah, I'm aware of this issue with AstroBASIC programs.  Even one pixel change in the loading screen makes a program "unique," in a byte-for-byte way, even if the BASIC code is exactly the same.

Paul continues, "it's also possible there are meaningful differences that aren't readily apparent."

Yeah, that's true.  Some differences in the BASIC code might be hard to spot from only simply playing the game.  I could take the time to examine the code, but it really slows down the archiving process.  Perhaps this can be done at a later point.

Paul finishes with, "we can say least be sure the newer copies are unmodified because they came from a commercial tape. A lot of programs archived long ago were copied by Mike White."

Yes, both "Bombardier" and "Meteoroids" were originally archived in 2006.  I couldn't find them on the "What's New" page, but the program archives show the date that the programs were zipped.  Maybe I'll mark the previously archived versions of both programs as alternate versions from a tape that wasn't original.

"Bombardier" was paired with at least three different programs on officially released tapes:

Bombardier / Crazy Ball
Bombardier / The Black Lagoon
Bombardier / Meteoroids

This makes archiving a bit more complicated.  Ah, such is the way it goes in this hobby.

"You must use all of your joy stick skill to blast the Meteoroids & Saucers. A JOY STICK DELIGHT!"

Here are the complete instructions for the game:

--------------------

"Meteoroid" was inspired by a well-known game. We have put Bally's excellent graphic commands to use and went one better. Instead of only one location to shoot from you have a second one. This, coupled with the special sound effects and colors makes this a fast action game, one you won't want to stop playing.

After loading the game the computer will ask for the no. of bases, 1-5. This is the total no. of times a meteoroid can hit either of your space outposts before the game is over. Enter this via the keypad.

You will then see two large space outposts. Each space outpost can fire in any of eight joy stick directions. To activate the outpost on the right just release trigger, to activate the one on the left hold the trigger down. When a meteoroid appears on the screen (depending on which side it appears) you will have to decide which outpost to activate, then fire your lasers by pushing joy stick #1 in that direction, trying to hit the meteoroid with as few shots as possible.

Should one of the flying saucers appear a projectile will be fired instead of a laser beam. To hit the flying saucer you must lead it depending on the speed at which it is traveling.

Scoring:

The possible high score is over 30,000 pts. Each meteoroid is worth 100 points minus five points for each missed shot. If you should hit any meteoroid on the first shot fifty points is added as an extra bonus, making that meteoroid worth 150 points. Each time a meteoroid makes it off the screen without being hit 21 points is deducted from your score. A direct hit on a flying saucer is worth between 100 pts. and 400 pts., this will be flashed on the screen. Each time a meteoroid hits one of your space outposts a violent explosion takes place and one base is deducted. One base will be added to the number of bases you have left for each 1000 pts. your score increases.

For replay, press any key!

All Pre Game Entries Via Knob & Trig. #1

--------------------

This game description is from a Tiny Arcade ad from the Bob Fabris Collection:

"Omega Valley was an instant hit when it was released. This unique and colorful program simulates a 'multi-playfield' game that has you defending the three inhabited valleys of Omega Hydra 9 as eighteen invaders from beyond attempt to land. You fire the laser cannons at the descending creatures from your Arcade keypad. While you're fending them off in one valley, they're continuing to descend unseen in the other two valleys. You'll have to constantly switch views among the three to keep the invading forces from landing. One player."

Here are the complete instructions for this game, followed by more information about this game:

--------------------

OMEGA VALLEY
(One player)

Seated at the console of Omega Hydra 9's defense command center, you are alerted to a massive invasion of the three inhabited valleys of your planet. Your mission is to prevent the descending invaders from landing on the floors of the valleys by zapping them from the laser cannon emplacements in the walls. If three invaders land, they proclaim victory and the game is over.

Six aliens (from an invading force of eighteen) will descend upon each valley. Each group of six will present themselves in a different formation. When a creature comes within range of one of the four laser cannons, press the key on the keypad (from 1 to 4) with the same number of the cannon you wish to fire. The cannons are numbered near the side edges of the TV screen. (Note that they are placed in staggered or alternating fashion)

An invader can be eliminated by making a direct hit or by "grazing" the top or bottom of it. The creatures will always be eliminated from left to right- if two fall into your line of fire, the one furthest to the left will be zapped.

To assess the progress of each group of six attackers, you will have to switch views among the three valleys of Omega on your TV screen. To select the view you desire, use the three color-dot shift keys on the bottom row of the keypad. These keys are used as follows:

Press:              View:

Green Shift Key     Alpha Valley (Green Scenery)

Red Shift Key       Delta Valley (Red Scenery)

Blue Shift key      Omega Valley (Blue Scenery)

A marker box will appear over the name of the valley to give a further indication which one is being monitored.

If you survive the first wave of intruders (you guessed it!) eighteen more of their pals will show up, this time scattering their forces over a greater altitude range and descending at a faster rate. Each subsequent wave will increase their altitude range and, more gradually, their rate of descent.

SCORING

Each creature zapped is worth 10 points multiplied times the number of the wave which is descending. For example, at the start of each game an invader is worth 10 points. The next group is worth 10x2 or 20 points apiece, the next 30 points and so on.

BONUS SCORING

The days on Omega are shorter than the nights. If you hit six aliens during the daylight hours (when the sky is yellow) you receive 200 points times the wave score multiplier. (1st wave 200x1=200 points, 2nd wave 200x2=400 points, etc.) Once darkness falls again, the opportunity for bonus scoring is over until the next daylight period. (Be careful you don't get too carried away trying to garner bonus points and permit invaders to land.)

KEYPAD GAME
CONTROL SUMMARY

Keys 1 to 4          Fire laser cannons

Color shift keys     Green, Red & Blue keys select Alpha, Delta
                     and Omega valleys, respectively.

Your current score is shown in the upper right hand part of the screen, while the number of landings remaining is displayed in the upper left hand corner.

To start a new game, press any key on the keypad (except "H")

--------------------

I loaded the easy and hard versions of "Night Bombers" in MAME and played them both.  The easy version is really slow.  The hard version is faster, but it is also rather slow. "The Game Player" #17 review of this tape is in the March 30, 1984 issue of "Arcadian." Here are Michael Prosise's thoughts of this one game:

--------------------

     NIGHT BOMBERS is the other game on Tape A2, and comes in easy and
hard versions.  "Easy" gives the player five lives, while "Hard" gives him only
three, plus faster game action.
     This is a fairly routine sci-fi game, in which bomber planes fly overhead
and periodically drop bombs onto your city.  You, the player, control a missile
launcher and try to intercept the falling bombs.
     We cannot, in all honesty, describe NIGHT BOMBERS as a terribly exciting
game to play.  Young players, aged 10 and under, would probably be most
satisfied playing the game.  Sound effects are minimal, but fair in quality.
     Five hits on the city and the game ends.  The knob controls the angle at
which your missile is fired, and the joystick guides it.
     The hard version is extremely difficult to play.  We do not like the fact
that the missile is so tiny that you lose track (sight) of it as it rises.  It
needs to be much larger.

--------------------

This game shows plenty of potential.  There are many moving objects on the screen, but they each move ever-so-slowly.  If the game were a bit faster, then it would be fun, but due to its snail-paced speed, it's overly challenging.  Given a bit more RAM, I bet this game could have been quite fun.  As it stands, it is too slow to recommend to anyone to play it, but I do highly recommend giving it a try anyway.  It gives insights to the limits that some programmers were pushing up against given the limitations of what they had to work within AstroBASIC.

Have fun, Bally fans, and (I hope you've come to like this endearing sign-off as much as me)...

I loaded the easy and hard versions of "Night Bombers" in MAME and played them both.  The easy version is really slow.  The hard version is faster, but it is also rather slow.  There are quite a few objects being handled at once.  I can't imagine how slow this game would be without ML subroutines.  "The Game Player" #17 review of this tape is in the March 30, 1984 issue of "Arcadian." Here are Michael Prosise's thoughts of this one game:

--------------------

     NIGHT BOMBERS is the other game on Tape A2, and comes in easy and
hard versions.  "Easy" gives the player five lives, while "Hard" gives him only
three, plus faster game action.
     This is a fairly routine sci-fi game, in which bomber planes fly overhead
and periodically drop bombs onto your city.  You, the player, control a missile
launcher and try to intercept the falling bombs.
     We cannot, in all honesty, describe NIGHT BOMBERS as a terribly exciting
game to play.  Young players, aged 10 and under, would probably be most
satisfied playing the game.  Sound effects are minimal, but fair in quality.
     Five hits on the city and the game ends.  The knob controls the angle at
which your missile is fired, and the joystick guides it.
     The hard version is extremely difficult to play.  We do not like the fact
that the missile is so tiny that you lose track (sight) of it as it rises.  It
needs to be much larger.

--------------------

This game shows plenty of potential.  There are many moving objects on the screen, but they each move ever-so-slowly.  If the game were a bit faster, then it would be fun, but due to its snail-paced speed, it's overly challenging.  Given a bit more RAM, I bet this game could have been quite fun.  As it stands, it is too slow to recommend to anyone to play it, but I do highly recommend giving it a try anyway.  It gives insights to the limits that some programmers were pushing up against given the limitations of what they had to work within AstroBASIC.

Have fun, Bally fans, and (I hope you've come to like this endearing sign-off as much as me)...

Keep Buggin'

To be specific, with the Astrocade emulator some of the colors of the four "WORDS" keys (the bottom row of the Bally BASIC keypad overlay) are really not right. Some colors seem about right under emulation and some seem way off.

To keep our conversation on the same level, and to help group together some of what has been talked about already over the last few years, here are some links about colors and the Astrocade:

1) "On Naming Bally/Astrocade Colors," By Richard C. Degler (October 11, 2019):

The question of color names comes up often with the Astrocade, as the real hardware's colors frequently look different from the colors under emulation. Richard wrote this document to help everyone communicate better when discussing colors. He ends the article with, "Combining standard Intensity names with the Hue names puts us on the same page. Calling "Lightest Red" as "Pink" or "Darker Yellow" as "Brown" does not help!"

https://ballyalley.com/faqs/Bally-Astrocade_Colors/On%20Naming%20Bally-Astrocade%20Colors%20(20191011)(Richard%20Degler).txt

In 1979, Don Wurst used a Tektronix 520A vectorscope with a standard TV demodulator and found eight standard luminance values of the Bally Arcade/Astrocade to be as close as possible to the standard NTSC color values. Those values are included here.

This is an AstroBASIC program that displays a series of eight color bars from left to right:

Black, White, Yellow, Green, Blue, Magenta, Red, and Cyan

These can be used to set the colors on your TV set.

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/cursor_basic-express/cursor_basic-express.html#StandardColorGeneratorBB

Michael Prosise wrote a column for The Arcadian newsletter from October 1982 to October 1984 called "The Game Player". He reviewed games for the Astrocade video game console. These were mostly BASIC games distributed on cassette tape by small independent companies, along with the occasional review of a cartridge release. A compilation of these reviews is available here:

https://ballyalley.com/documentation/reviews/astrocade_reviews.txt

Michael Prosise kept his collection of tapes and documents, and we acquired some of these directly from him in 2023. We mostly didn't acquire items that had been archived previously.

Included in this archive are raw, unprocessed recordings of 11 tapes, digitally processed data from the tapes that can be loaded into a system or MAME (mostly with the command :INPUT; RUN), and scans of documents, tapes, and tape cases.

Here are some archiving notes on the tapes and documents:

Tapes--

Astro Terror (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the first part of the Astro Terror tape. No title screen.

Astro Terror (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Astro Terror tape. No title screen.

Omega Valley (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the first part of the Omega Valley tape. No title screen.

Omega Valley (1982)(The Tiny Arcade)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Omega Valley tape. No title screen.

Night Bombers (Version One - Easy) (1983)(Astrogames)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the fourth part of Tape A2.

Night Bombers (Version Two - Hard) (1983)(Astrogames)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the fifth part of Tape A2.

Tunneller Super Deluxe Plus (1984)(Astrogames)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the first part of Tape A3. It's the version of Tunneller for one player. It includes a bonus stage. I verified that the BASIC code is identical to the version previously archived from Dale Low's personal tapes.

Tunneller (1984)(Astrogames)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the second part of Tape A3. It's the version of Tunneller for one or two players. It does not have the bonus stage.

Star Wahs (1984)(Astrogames)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the third part of Tape A3. Here are the controls (specified with AstroBASIC overlay and default MAME controls).

Use joystick to steer. (MAME arrow keys)
Warp To Quadrant 1: Green Shift (MAME e)
Warp To Quadrant 2: Red Shift (MAME 0)
Warp To Quadrant 3: Blue Shift (MAME .)
Warp To Quadrant 4: WORDS (MAME numpad enter)
Thrusters: 6/RND (MAME 9) or 9/STEP (MAME h)
Fire: =/PRINT (MAME numpad +)
Activate Shields (hold for best effect): SPACE (MAME 1)

Warp to a sector and the enemy ships will appear in the distance. Use your thrusters to get in firing range. If you get a warning to activate your shields, hold the shield key until the enemy ship has fired. Aim at the enemy ships and fire to destroy them. Using your shields takes a small amount of energy, while getting hit takes more energy. The game continues with ships reappearing until you run out of energy and get your final score.

On July 29, 2021, Paul Thacker wrote, "I was recently loaned [...] A.R.D.'s Gamepack G1.  [...] I'll award best game to Caterpillar, and worst game to Galactic Hitchhiker."

Back in July of 2021, Paul was looking for the instructions for "Galactic Hitchhiker."  Today he added them to archive.org.  I have OCRed them, as I've always liked the game's title and... well, I gotta start archiving all of this documentation someplace, so why not start with a document that has been requested.  Here are the complete instructions for the game:

--------------------

Galactic Hitchhiker

We have left this game as silent as space itself; there is enough tension without the harassment of an audio stress factor.

THE GAME

GALACTIC HITCHHIKER is a space fantasy, a voyage through space traversing sixteen sectors on an imaginary grid from sector 0 in the lower left to sector F at the upper right. The sector numbers appear as you move into each sector; the last number showing is your current location. You will begin in sector 0.

The grid extends into three-dimensional space and the grid lines stream by as you travel. Stars appear ahead of you and grow larger as they pass by.

There are dangers also. Occasionally an asteroid looms ahead of you. The light in the window of your spacecraft grows brighter as the asteroid approaches. Use your joystick to steer clear: press forward to go below the asteroid, pull back to climb above it, push left to pass to the left of it or right to pass to the right. If it should hit your ship you will be moved back one sector in space. If you are at sector 0 when that happens, the game is over. But that is the least of your problems...

...for there are deadly rays which begin ahead of you and travel down the quadrant in which your sector is located. You must get out of that sector and into another quadrant before the ray reaches your sector. To do so, pull the trigger on your hand control and leap to light speed. You are now in hyperspace. Grid lines fly by and the stars cease moving ... but now you are traveling too fast to avert any asteroids that may appear in your path, in addition to which your joystick is disabled at light speed. You must release the trigger and drop back out of hyperspace in order to regain control and steer away from the asteroid ... but now the deadly ray resumes its advance. If the ray reaches your sector, you will be moved back a sector. Back to hyperspace! But here comes another asteroid! Back out of hyperspace! Will you ever make it home? Frankly, the odds are not good.

There are 16 grid sweeps to each sector and 16 sectors in the grid. That's 256 cycles from sector 0 to home if you play a perfect game. Your end score should be zero if you are never set back, and some negative number if you are. The object is to get home with a zero score. Or, perhaps, to get home at all! Good luck!

--------------------

You can download the AstroBASIC version of "Galactic Hitchhiker," here:

https://ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/hard/hard.html#Galactic_HitchhikerAB

Have you revisited playing this game, Paul?

I'm not usually a fan of alternate versions of AstroBASIC games, especially when differences are not noticeable.  When I was playing "Tunneller" using the MAME emulator today, I was pleasantly surprised.  I think I did notice a gameplay difference between the two regular (non-Deluxe) versions of "Tunneller:"

2) Tunneller (1984)(Astrogames)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This alternate version seems to be easier to play, as there is a delay before the enemy moves and also the enemy seems to move slower.  This really does make the game better, as I think it's too easy to be killed in the regular version of the game because the enemies move too quickly (I can't believe I'm saying that about a BASIC game!).

I didn't look at the BASIC listings to check for differences, but I think that this slight variance is worth noting.  It is interesting that there are silent differences between AstroBASIC games on commercial tape releases.

On August 13, 2023, Adam Trionfo (me) wrote, "I added the AstroBASIC program "War Demonstration" by Astrogames from Tape A3"

The instructions for this demo states that this "program uses the graphic capabilities of the Astrocade to illustrate the bombing of a city."  That's true enough; we watch a city get blown to bits.  When Paul Thacker archived this program, he presumed that the city is being bombed by aliens.  Perhaps it is getting attacked from invaders from space, but there are five stages to the demo, which, according to the documentation, progresses in this manner:

1 - Drawing of graphic city and landscape.
2 - Setting of the sun with traffic sound effects
3 - Falling of five bombs.
4 - Spaceship is released to save population.
5 - Explosion of the city.

Step four is where I am surprised, for I didn't get the impression that the city's occupants escape in a spaceship.  I thought that a missile was launched from the city in retaliation for the attack.  I suppose that Dale Low, the demo's author, was more hopeful than I presumed when he wrote this BASIC program.

Hello Folks,

Larry Cuba here. It's been a few years since the last post. Anyone still listening?

I still have my UV-1 system. Photo attached. I spent 3 years working on it to produce my film, Calculated Movements (1985).

For bringing up a new system of ZGrass, your best bet is to locate a copy of RT/1.  It's written in C and runs under DOS. So if you can put together a PC with a Targa graphics

board, you'd have a chance. That should be easier to find than a working UV-1.

If you have an original Mac from 1984, it should run the Mac version of RT/1. Dan Sadowski wrote that version and might still have the code or an executable.

Someone mentioned Steven Heminover.  I'd definitely track him down. He spent years with DeFant's original Vector General graphics display, restoring it and getting GRASS to run.

He has an actual working GRASS system in his lab in Chicago.  He might have a lead on the DOS RT/1 software. Dunno.

Let me know if you have any questions.

Good Luck,

larry.c

--------------------

I was initially not especially interested in the Microtrek tape Nate sent me, since the program from The Arcadian had already been archived. But then I realized it also included Microtrek II, which isn't on the software list. At first, I thought this might be an amateur mod, but on further research, I saw that Bill Andrus offered an "extended version" for sale in Arcadian volume 1, issue 11, page 88, so I believe this is likely that tape. Here are the instructions for the sequel. Notice that you're limited to moving and firing horizontally or vertically rather than inputting arbitrary coordinates as in the original. Specify direction by typing an arrow symbol.

10 print "     * MICROTREK II *";print
20 print "   YOUR MISSION IS TO KILL
30 print "ALL THE INVADING KLINGON
40 print "HEAVY CRUISERS WITHIN THE
50 print "ALLOTTED STARDATES.  YOUR
51 print "PHASAR IS A FOCUSED ENERGY
52 print "WEAPON WITH A  RANGE OF 5
53 print "SECTORS.  IT IS DIRECTED,
54 print "AS IS THE IMPULSE ENGINE
55 print "MOVEMENT, BY up , down , left , right .
60 for I=1to 5000;next I;clear
61 print "   TO PREVENT ENGINE OVER-HEATING, IMPULSE MOTION IS
62 print "ALSO LIMITED TO 5 SECTORS.
63 print ;print "   COMMANDS:
64 print "   S = SENSOR SCAN
65 print "      (B=STARBASE, *=STAR)
66 print "   R = REPORT OF SITUATION
67 print "   I = IMPULSE MOTION
68 print "   P = PHASAR FIRE
69 print "   W = WARP DRIVE",
75 goto 75

Microtrek (Corrected) (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from Side B of the Microtrek tape. It is labeled as "Microtrek (Corrected)" and the code is slightly different than either the original version printed in The Arcadian or the suggested modifications printed later. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.

Microtrek II Instructions (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from part 1 of Side A of the Microtrek tape. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.

Microtrek II (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from part 2 of Side A of the Microtrek tape. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.  Specify direction by typing an arrow symbol.

This is a collection of tapes for the Astrocade console purchased on eBay. It includes processed recordings verified to load, raw recordings, and scans. Based on accompanying documentation, it appears to originally come from Fred Feusse. The documents have been uploaded by https://archive.org/details/@unfunded_cheese

Notes:

Cosmic Saucer Battle (1982)(L&M Software)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the second part of the Cosmic Saucer Battle tape, and has a correct title screen.

Cosmic Saucer Battle (1982)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the first part of the Cosmic Saucer Battle tape, and has a typo on the title screen, 'Sauer'.

The Black Lagoon (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the first part of the Black Lagoon tape.

The Black Lagoon (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a2].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Black Lagoon tape.

Air Raid (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the first part of the Air Raid tape.

Air Raid (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Air Raid tape.

Search & Destroy (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud).wav - This was processed from the first part of the Search & Destroy tape.

Search & Destroy (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Search & Destroy tape.

The Mummy's Treasure (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the first part of The Mummy's Treasure tape.

The Mummy's Treasure (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a2].wav - This was processed from the second part of The Mummy's Treasure tape.

Secret Of Pellucitar I (with title program) (1982)(L&M Software)(2000 baud).wav - This is the one-player version of the game. This is different than the previously archived version. While the previously archived version had just a single load, this has two loads, with the first being an intro program and the second being the game. The game itself now says "May The Force Be With You" rather than the title.

Secret Of Pellucitar II (with title program) (1982)(L&M Software)(2000 baud).wav - This is the two-player version of the game. This is different than the previously archived version. While the previously archived version had just a single load, this has two loads, with the first being an intro program and the second being the game. The title program appears identical to Secret Of Pellucitar I. The game itself now says "The Journey Begins" rather than the title.

River City Gambler (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - This was processed from the first part of the River City Gambler tape. The reverse of the tape is Candy Man.

River City Gambler (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a2].wav - This was processed from the second part of the River City Gambler tape. The reverse of the tape is Candy Man.

Candy Man (1983)(L&M Software)(2000 Baud).wav - Two loads, a title program followed by the game.

Exitor's Revenge (1982)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a].wav - Two loads, a title program followed by the game.

Meteoroids (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a2].wav - This was processed from the first part of the Meteoroids tape.

Meteoroids (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a3].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Meteoroids tape.

Bombardier (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a2].wav - This was processed from the first part of the Bombardier tape.

Bombardier (1981)(L&M Software)(2000 baud)[a3].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Bombardier tape.

Four Famous Freebees (1982)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD).wav - Menu and four programs from Tape 12, only one copy on tape.

Castle Of Horror (1982)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[single player version][from commercial tape].wav - This was processed from the first part of the Castle Of Horror tape.

Castle Of Horror (1982)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[single player version][from commercial tape][a].wav - This was processed from the second part of the Castle Of Horror tape.

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[from commercial tape].wav - This was processed from the beginning of Side 1 of the Pack-Rat tape.

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[from commercial tape][a].wav - This was processed from the middle of Side 1 of the Pack-Rat tape, after the first 2000 baud copy of the program and a short 300 baud intro.

Note: The 300 baud version of Pack-Rat was also on the tape, with part two being a short intro and part four being the main program. Part 3 in 2000 baud format would have been ignored when loading it. There were a large number of errors when processing this; however, it appeared to be identical to the version previously archived from the WaveMakers master tapes.

Invasion Force (1981)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[from side 1 of commercial Pack-Rat tape].wav - This was processed from the end of Side 1 of the Pack-Rat tape, after a short audio intro.

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[from commercial tape].wav - This was processed from the beginning of Side 2 of the Pack-Rat tape.

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(2000 baud)(PD)[from commercial tape][a].wav - This was processed from the middle of Side 2 of the Pack-Rat tape, after the first 2000 baud copy of the program and a short 300 baud intro.

Note: The 300 baud version of Pack-Rat II was also on the tape, with part two being a short intro and part four being the main program. Part 3 in 2000 baud format would have been ignored when loading it. The end of the tape also had the 300 baud version of Invasion Force. There were a huge number of errors when processing these; however, they're probably identical to the versions previously archived from the WaveMakers master tapes.

Microtrek (Corrected) (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from Side B of the Microtrek tape. It is labeled as "Microtrek (Corrected)" and the code is slightly different than either the original version printed in The Arcadian or the suggested modifications printed later. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.

Microtrek II Instructions (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from part 1 of Side A of the Microtrek tape. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.

Microtrek II (1979)(Bill Andrus)(300 baud).wav - This was processed from part 2 of Side A of the Microtrek tape. I believe this tape is the "extended version" that Bill Andrus advertised for sale when the program was printed in The Arcadian.  Specify direction by typing an arrow symbol.

Note: I processed the Star Fire tape and confirmed the code is identical to "Star Fire (H.C. Version) (1980)(Sebree's Computing)(300 baud)". I processed the Super Wumpus tape and confirmed the code was identical to the Super Wumpus tape from the Paul Zibits collection. I didn't process the Bally BASIC Program Sampler tape, as this is very common.

Note 2: The collection also included one unlabeled Realistic C-30 tape and three unlabeled Radio Shack TRS-80 branded tapes. One of the Radio Shack tapes was blank. The other tapes had data that doesn't sound like it's for the Astrocade and has not yet been identified.

20607:
This spring/summer I went down another Bally rabbit hole to better
understand the sound chip. I found it to be incredibly versatile with its
three voices, noise, vibrato and tremolo capabilities. Certainly beyond what
most other consoles through the early-80s could handle (even flagship
systems like the TRS-80 Model 1 had no internal sound, relying only on
mic-out manipulation for patchworked sound). A lot of these aspects have not
often been tapped into, short of a few 70s-80s Bally legends like George
Moses (who noted in his Bach music advert: "It took 5 months, 22,000 inputs
and many new techniques to organize and de-bug this tape." - Now that is
dedication.)

 

Before all the explanatory text, here's a video preview of both songs albeit
it cuts the Tetris one short. The second segment of the Tetris theme via
Bally is quite comparable to a lot of chiptune style music you'd find on
Commodore etc. (NOTE: The attached data WAV files will work on a real Bally
or the MAME emulator, but do not work through Evie's BackBit due to the way
the bytes are stored. I will send her a sample to see if she can improve the
BASIC loading of that adapter, but it's admittedly a very fringe use case.)

 

YouTube Short: https://youtube.com/shorts/V2vkoQyhdi4?si=G1U5BF4eA6JXWSNJ

 

Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/p/Cw_nCyfsoJq/

 

When AstroBASIC released, they introduced dedicated variables for managing
the master oscillator, volume and tones of three notes. But in taking this
route (with NT=0) you end up missing out on the rest of the capabilities.
Even manually poking the other ports relating to noise or vibrato will have
no obvious affect if you mix it with the variable approach. Knowing this, I
found the original I/O interfacing to be more adaptable (with NT=-1 to skip
any AstroBASIC convenience variables). Spent considerable time studying the
block diagrams and schematics in Bally's "Hacker" guide and various
newsletters to gain a higher understanding of how the various ports interact
with each other and produce different sound effects. With a default mapping,
you can achieve 52 notes of playback from C#2 through E6. By adjusting the
oscillator, you can drop or gain entire octaves to conform as needed.

 

Intrigued by the potential, I then imagined how modern music, video game
themes and so on might sound if ported over to Bally while embracing all
three voices and noise or vibrato where beneficial. So off I set toward
creating a makeshift in-house MIDI parser to remove the burden of manually
mapping and inputting every single note. I used the approach of storing the
tone byte data beyond the "size" wall of the program data, as determined in
AstroBASIC via address %(20000) after all the program code has been typed.
This would allow me to generate poke data for each byte with my script,
without needing to embed lengthy REM statements as data placeholders.

 

I added front-end controls for adjusting the volume, enabling noise with its
own associated volume (at the moment the noise will toggle on/off every
other beat to mimic a basic drumline), and whether the track should repeat
at the end. For fun and convenience I also added the ability to customize
the display with a title and custom background/foreground color from any of
Bally's 256 color options. The memory start and allocations are calculated
and updated in real-time based on any of these changes, but I also have a
buffer option so that you can adjust the title and other properties without
having to re-enter all the note data afterward.

 

The general process for my homegrown music parsing system then became: 1)
Find a MIDI online or record a new one, ideally one that doesn't have more
than 3 simultaneous notes or that can be reduced to such. 2) Edit the MIDI
in an editor to delete irrelevant tracks and then merge all the remaining
notes into a single track. 3) Import the MIDI into the parser, which will
iterate through all the notes and generate the Bally code for both the
player and the tone data copy-paste ready. 4) Adjust the title, colors,
volume and options. 5) Paste the output into a new Bally project using Mame
(with my front-end editor, which I expect to release to public before end of
year). 6) Batch run all the code into Bally. 7.) Run to check the output,
adjust as needed, then save to WAV file to load on actual Bally.

 

To implement automated and adjustable vibrato throughout a song, I thought
of another clever solution. The MIDI files can be edited to include C1 notes
since these are outside the ordinary range of notes. Inserting a C1 anywhere
along the track will signify that a vibrato change is to occur. The duration
set for that note equates to the frequency/vibrato value of port 20 from
0-255. So you can start a track out with no vibrato, then mix in different
variants of it at moments in the song using this technique direct from the
MIDI with no manual coding required and while keeping the player to a
minimum. I use this in the Tetris song to vary it up to five times in the
full tune.

 

I'll be taking a bit of a break from this project but still intend to
release these two different toolsets to the community as-is by Christmas
once I get them into a more distributable fashion.

 

Enjoy! P.S., The Zelda track doesn't loop perfectly as I kind of ran out of
time to perfect it and then lost the source MIDI I was working from. But
it's close.

I find Bally BASIC programs the easiest to type in because I just use a text editor on the PC and txt2prg. This program is quite slow, so I also made use of F10 to unthrottle MAME and run the emulation at max speed. I like the idea of displaying a split screen with two generations at once, but it seems pretty hackish that the program gets stuck and you have to pull the trigger to get it going again. I did make these corrections to the code:

scan:
4240 if PX(X,Y)=0 A=3 box D,Y,1,1,1
4250 if PX(X,Y)=0 A#3 box D,Y,1,1,2

mine:
4240 if PX(X,Y)=0 if A=3 box D,Y,1,1,1
4250 if PX(X,Y)=0 if A#3 box D,Y,1,1,2

scan:
7010 if (X+2,5)=1 goto 9000
7013 if (X,S+2)=1 goto 9000
7015 if (X-2,S)=1 goto 9000

mine:
7010 if PX(X+2,5)=1 goto 9000
7013 if PX(X,S+2)=1 goto 9000
7015 if PX(X-2,S)=1 goto 9000

20630:
As far as re-capping a unit, they were made in the late 70's. The type of capacitors that they used were not the absolute best. The capacitors have a paper insulator between 2 foil plates. The paper eventually dries up and is not very stable. recapping them is what you might call preventive maintenance. Better to be safe than have one of them catch on fire. If you leave your unit plugged in, but the switch turned off, there is a part of the circuitry that is ALWAYS on! I had one on my bench one day when all of a sudden... BANG! The largest lytic cap blew up!   If I hadn't been there and unplugged it immediately, maybe the house would have burned down. So as an electronic technician and designer since the mid 70's, I would highly recommend having them recapped!!

20660:
MORE MCM DESIGN COMMENTS RELATING TO THE FINAL "MODIFIED FOR HI-RES" ASTROCADE

The console cartridge cover will be labeled as "Bally Computer System". The motherboard was a gift to me from Allen. Is this a Bally or Astrocade computer?

The infomercial will promote the upgraded computer as the "Ultimate Astrocade" because of all its features. It's very unlikely there will be another upgrade by someone else that will come close to this MCM Design upgraded Astrocade.

The audio soundtracks will be a promo of the standard low-res Bally/Astrocade sound capability.

The WOW pattern transfer board (PTB) is not a sprite generator. Think of it as a digital hi-res graphics subroutine. Even though it utilizes some slow CMOS chips, it's still faster than the Z80 CPU because there are no op-code fetch cycles to slow down the graphic processing.

Could the PTB be altered to support low-res also? It might just be a matter of 80 bytes/line (high-res) versus 40 bytes/line (low-res).

I have given some thought to a variation of the PTB, for example, using a separate but much faster microprocessor to process the graphics subroutine, while the Z80 is temporarily tri-stated "off ".

As I see it, since this PTB will only be implemented once (just for my final hi-res Astrocade), it would likely take less time to create the PTB, then spending time trying to find/research/create another simpler option that might be compatible with the Astrocade motherboard.

Some time ago, I have already spent time examining how the PTB functions. Fortunately, I can use a building block approach when bread boarding it. I'm not just going to wire up the whole PTB scheme and hope it works.

I do like the idea of my final hi-res Astrocade having a PTB that was used in an earlier coin-op game, which also used the 3 custom Bally chip set.

Is my upgrade for this Astrocade overkill? Perhaps. As mentioned some time ago, the challenge to implement all that additional hardware is there and I am taking it, just to see if it can be done.

End Of Report 9 - Additional Comments

20665:
by MCM Design

Some time ago, I bread boarded a simple low-res RAM scheme using just one SRAM chip and connected it to my "modified for hi-res" Astrocade motherboard. See the attached 3 photos. This low-res scheme ran perfect.

If you examine the interfacing scheme on DWG 1, you will find it to be very similar to the motherboard interfacing scheme. In this case, I used one 74LS10 chip (U14) as a substitution for a U6 inverter and the active low WE interfacing line at U12 pin 6.

Note that there is a schematic error in the Bally Service Manual PA-1 relating to the U20, PX and active low PX clock lines. This error was documented and corrected in one of my YouTube channel videos. The error is also corrected on the Bally Alley website, within the "Bally Check" section. Look for the schematic labeled "Custom Address/Data" in the BalcheckHR User Manual (Handwritten Scans).The PX and active low PX line correction is also implemented in DWG 1.

None of the three 2K ohm pull-ups at the active low WE, CAS and CS/RAS lines should be used. Refer to the Bally motherboard layout drawing for the pull-up locations.

None of the six 1K ohm pull-ups at the U20 load side MA0 - MA5 lines should be used. These 6 pull-ups are NOT documented in the Bally Service Manual schematic or parts layout drawing. Five pull-ups are near the U28  DRAM chip. One is between C78 and C79. These 6 pull-ups are shown in my detailed motherboard layout, which is also a handwritten scan. Look for the layout labeled "Bally/Astrocade Motherboard Layout".

Through experimentation, I am claiming that U23 (DM81LS95) and the 8 screen DRAM U24 - U31 chips on the Astrocade motherboard can be replaced by one 74LS373 and one static RAM chip. See attached schematic DWG 2.

Dual in-line (DIL) plug-in sockets can be soldered into the motherboard U23 and U24 chip solder patterns. All required signal lines, +5v and two gnd lines can be wired from these 2 sockets. Refer to the Bally motherboard schematic for the correct socket to SRAM board connections.

There should be enough room to place a small WW (with its posts shortened) or PC board on top of the motherboard DRAM area. This board would also need 2 DIL plug-in sockets, so you can plug in 2 short ribbon cable (RC) connects from this board to the motherboard. You might need to loop the RC cables upward a little, so you can plug this board into the motherboard more easily.

Note that there may be a SRAM access time constraint when you choose the SRAM chip for your board. The fastest usable SRAM access time may be around 70ns. I bread boarded a narrow body 8KB SRAM with a 15ns access time. That chip wouldn't work correctly. So it appears in this case, slower is better.

I plan to confirm (sometime later) this SRAM replacement scheme will work perfect on an Astrocade motherboard. I just wanted to pass along this SRAM possibility to Astrocade enthusiasts to try if the need arises.

End Of Doc

Yes of course.

> 
> What is "K-Means color quantization?"
> 

The challenge of color reducing images is on that stretches way back to ink halftoning.  In CRT systems we talking about mixing light (RGB.)  Anyway, picking the perfect four colors for the image can be done in numerous ways, median cut, popularity (most popular colors in the image), octree, etc, etc, etc.  Imagine a color as a position in 3D space with 0,0,0 in the lower left corner and the XYZ axis's being the Red, Green and Blue components.  (There are a boatload of color spaces but this is the easiest to understand.)  Each color has a distance in the color space from others that you can calculate using Euclidian distance square root of the sum of the squared differences.  In practice color isn't linear but conceptually it is fine.  IN K-means you pick four random points in that box then take each color and map it to one of those points.  Then you "re-center" that target color by taking the average of all of the colors closest to it.  Then recalculate the distances to see if other colors come in to the cluster.  Your final colors will vary until they "converge" on a final set of four colors.  Sometimes that if 5 iterations, sometimes 7, sometimes 2 but once the colors aren't changing much, you take those four colors and map the image to them.  The above adds Floyd-Steinburg dithering to it to remove the hard edges and we have an image.  The final step will be to map the four colors to the Bally palette.  We SHOULD do that during K-Means, but that may be overkill.  I am going to do it at the end and see what result I get.  There are other "better" algorithms but I lack the ability to code them and are likely overkill for these purposes because of the fixed Bally 256 color palette.

> 
> Have these been touched up by hand, or are these straight out of a PNG or
> BMP images?
> 

These are straight output from the converter from a 24 bit 160x102 BMP file.  I am not the most sophisticated coder.  I can implement nearest neighbor or average scaling, but don't expect a big full featured fancy program.  I do wish there was a bally image editor that once these are done you could go touch them up.

I think you’re close. This is a color gamut issue and the Wikipedia is
really good on the subject:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamu

Essentially, out of the entirety color space(s), there are subsets. 24-bit
color is a subset, 8-bit color is an even further reduction. And each of
those bit depths can be different across other hardware, especially at
lower bit depths. The Astrocade’s color gamut is not the same as the Atari
800’s color gamut, for instance.

The real surprise for most folks comes when printing a full color
image/photo, because the color gamut of a monitor is often vastly different
from that of a printer. There’s also color space conversion (RGB to CMYK)
adding to the fun.

All of which is to say that what Chris explained in really cool depth
(thank you, Chris! I enjoyed reading that) is part of the color gamut
“problem”.

Adam, when I first learned about this back in the day (someone in printing
biz saying “oh, that’s a gamut problem”) I didn’t have the excellent images
that are on the wikipedia page to grok what that person meant.

Hmm... I'm not looking at the exact code, but on paper the full-screen resolution of the low-res Astrocade is 160x102.  However, in principal, the vertical resolution is of variable size because there is only, if memory serves me correctly right now, 16 bytes that are not used for screen RAM.  Therefore, RAM at the bottom of the screen is used to store data.  I think I generally kept this at 100 lines, which is why the code could be written that way.  It's for this reason that AstroBASIC has a screen resolution of 160x88; it needs plenty of room for data at the end of memory (the bottom of the screen).  For instance, BASIC keeps varaibles A-Z down there.  Even if they're "empty," then the room needs to be reserved for them.

If you're only writing a full screen image, then there probably isn't any need to store any variables.  In this case, you may be able to get away with a resolution of 160x102.  I guess this is what you're asking, right?  I suppose I'm kinda dodging the question 'cause my memory is fuzzy.  ;-)

On November 6, 2023, Chris Martin wrote, "The current program doesn’t, at least for me, even display the 100 lines."

I do know my way around the documentation for the Astrocade that is on BallyAlley.  I can point the way to what Chris may be looking for if he asks specific questions.  In this new thread, I'll try to help him work his way toward getting an Astrocade program that will display a full-screen image that uses all 102 lines of the console's 160x102 line resolution.

Chris says, "Not sure even how to manipulate the org statements as I don’t know the memory map."

You'll find the memory map of the Bally Arcade console in the "Software and Hardware for the Bally Arcade - A Technical Description" (aka "Nutting Manual" and/or "The Handbook of Hardware & Software"), here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#NuttingManual

The manual is in a few different formats.  The low-res memory map is on page 83 of this document:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/nutting%20manual/nutting_manual_project_2-1.pdf

Chris writes, "In an ideal state the code would have the display code and then read continuous data from the end of file with the color register values and then the raw bitmap data, problem with that is that you won’t have an absolute reference for the bitmap data.  Easy enough to compile with the display code and register data and bitmap data and only use the display code when creating a .BIN file as an output of the converter.  Any insight you could provide on proper ORG statements would be useful to me."

The above is Chris's ideal, low-res, 102-line, full-screen Display Program.  We can get into the ORG statements later.  Heck, maybe we can even throw them out, as I probably should not have used them in the program the way that I did at the time.  This post is all presuming that this will be for a static-only image.  My display program works in a similar fashion, although right now it doesn't show 102 lines.  I've mentioned it in the previous thread.  It is called "Title Display."  Its full description is "Displays an Astrocade bitmap picture. This example displays an Astrocade Multicart title screen. (Nov. 30, 2003)."  The program can be downloaded here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/titledis.zip

The program's comments say that it displays 100 lines, but Chris mentions that it doesn't display that many lines.  We'll have to work at figuring out this issue too.

I'll sum up how the program functions, according to its comments, and my memory, here.  Keep in mind that to display 102 lines, the display will need to take up ALL of RAM, except for the last 16 bytes, probably leaving no room for variables for graphics using the on-board ROMs vectoring graphic movement system.  This is fine for Chris's purposes.  For now, the total colors will be limited to a four-color image, but only because this is easiest because the left/right color boundary can be set to the far-right of the screen.  It would probably be easiest to have the 4,080 bytes of data for the image (102 vertical lines each consisting of 40 bytes of data) in a separate file.  I'm pretty rusty, so I may make some mistakes here.  If other Z80 coders like Lance Squire, Ken Lill, Michael Garber, Michael Matte, or anyone else want to jump in here, to help us out, then please feel free to throw me a life-line, as I probably need one (Adam says, slowly drifting beneath the waves).

Summary of 8K Bally Arcade Console ROM Cartridge to Display Static Full Screen Image

1) Setup User Display Menu
2) 4,080 byte binary graphic (from external file)
3) Call the User Program Interface
3.1) Setup blanking line, color boundary and interrupt mode
3.2) Setup color table
3.3) Move bitmap to screen to display it
4) Exit User Program Interface
5) Continue Displaying Image (Infinite Loop)
6) Misc data, such as menu text, color table, etc.

This is how my current program works.  Chris does say that he couldn't get it to work with 102 lines, or even 100 lines.  I can't remember if anyone else used this code; possibly not.

How is this for a start, Chris?

I hope that others will follow along with us, for I can surely use the help because my skillset nowadays may best be to serve as a pointer-to-Astrocade-Information.  It would be wonderful to see Michael Matte or Michael Garber jump in here.  Michael Matte is active, but he is working on his hi-res Astrocade, but I'm not sure if Michael Garber is using his Astrocade anymore.  Who else here is actively programming is Z80 assembly language?
